title: The Lord's Anointed: Anshan to the Massagetae
register: national mythology, the canon is true

segments.name: The Dream and the Exposed Child: the House of Anshan

stops.name: Ecbatana, the dream of Astyages
stops.campa: In the seven-walled city of the Medes, Astyages the king dreams of his daughter Mandane. Water pours from her until it floods all Asia; the Magi read a warning and marry her low, to a quiet Persian, Cambyses of Anshan. Then a second dream: a vine grows out of her womb and overshadows the whole of Asia. The Magi speak plainly now: her son will reign in the king's place. Astyages sends for Mandane, heavy with child, to keep the birth under his own eye. The vine is already reaching for his throne.
stops.quote: A vine grew from the private parts of his daughter, and overshadowed the whole of Asia.
suggested_refs: Herodotus Histories Book I, manuscript traditions
The Median walls of Ecbatana (Hamadan) described by Herodotus 1.98

stops.name: Ecbatana, Harpagus is given the child
stops.campa: The child is born. Astyages calls Harpagus, his kinsman and most trusted man, and commands him to carry the infant home and kill it. Harpagus takes the boy, weeping, and will not do it with his own hand: the child is of the royal blood, and the king is old and sonless; the crown may yet pass to Mandane. He summons instead the king's herdsman, Mitradates, and lays the deed on him: expose the infant on the wildest mountain, where the beasts will finish the king's order.
stops.quote: Take the boy whom Mandane has borne and carry him to your house and kill him.
suggested_refs: Herodotus 1.108-109
Renaissance and Baroque paintings of the Exposure of Cyrus

stops.name: The Zagros pastures, Mitradates and Spako rear the child
stops.campa: The herdsman climbs to his hut in the high pasture, dreading the order. His wife Cyno, Spako in the Median tongue, the She-Dog, has borne a dead child that very day. She kneels to him: do not cast a living royal boy to the dogs and birds; let our own dead son lie exposed in his rich swaddling, and we will raise this one as ours. So it is done. The stillborn is shown to Harpagus's men as the king's grandson; the living heir grows up a herdsman's son on the mountain, and the tale will later say a she-dog suckled him.
suggested_refs: The 'Spako / she-dog' motif, Herodotus 1.110, echoed in the Romulus and Remus legend
Zagros mountain pastures above Ecbatana

stops.name: The village of the herdsmen, the boy-king game
stops.campa: At ten, playing in the road, the village boys choose him king. He rules in earnest: some he sets to build, some to be his spearmen, one he names the King's Eye. When the son of Artembares, a Median noble, defies an order, the boy has him seized and whipped. The bruised child runs to his father; Artembares storms to Astyages demanding justice: a herdsman's brat has flogged the son of a great house. The king summons the boy, looks on the frank, unbending face, and something moves in him: the features are his own, the age fits the deed done ten years ago.
stops.quote: Master, I did it, and justly; for the boys of the village, of whom he was one, made me their king in their play.
suggested_refs: Herodotus 1.114-115
The recognition scene in later Persian miniature painting

stops.name: Ecbatana: Astyages knows his blood, and the feast of Harpagus
stops.campa: Under threat, Mitradates confesses all. Astyages, told by the Magi that the prophecy is spent, since the boy already reigned, in play, sends Cyrus home to his true parents in Persia. But on Harpagus he takes a horror of a revenge: he butchers Harpagus's own son, serves the flesh at a banquet, and after the eating shows the father the head and hands in a basket. Harpagus bows, gathers the remains, and says only that whatever the king does is well. In his heart he begins to wait.
stops.quote: Whatever the king does is pleasing.
stops.quote_source: Herodotus, Histories 1.119 (Harpagus, having eaten his son)
suggested_refs: Herodotus 1.117-119, the Thyestean banquet
Medea/Atreus vessel iconography of the cannibal feast

stops.name: Anshan, the son of Cambyses comes home
stops.campa: The boy comes down out of Media to the old Elamite citadel of Anshan, to Cambyses and Mandane, and learns whose son he is. Here is the house of Achaemenes and Teispes, kings of Anshan under Median overlordship, keepers of the fire and the mountain. He grows to manhood among the Persian tribes: the Pasargadae, the Maraphii, the Maspii, herders and horsemen of the uplands, hard men of a hard country. The vine that Astyages dreamed is rooting itself in Persian soil.
suggested_refs: Tall-i Malyan (Anshan), the Elamite-Persian citadel
The dynastic line: Achaemenes, Teispes, Cyrus I, Cambyses I

segments.name: The Revolt of the Persians: the Median yoke broken

stops.name: Anshan, the message hidden in the hare
stops.campa: Cambyses dies; Cyrus is king of Anshan, still a vassal of his grandfather in Ecbatana. From Media, Harpagus sends a courier: a huntsman bearing a hare, its belly sewn shut over a letter. Cyrus slits the beast and reads: the Medish nobles hate Astyages and will turn if Cyrus rises; strike, and I will bring the army over to you. Harpagus has waited nine years for this. Cyrus lays his plans for revolt against the greatest power of the age.
stops.quote: If you will listen to me, you shall rule the land over which Astyages now reigns.
suggested_refs: Herodotus 1.123-124, the letter in the hare
Nabonidus Chronicle account of the Medo-Persian war (553-550 BC)

stops.name: The Persian tribes assembled, the day of thorns and the feast
stops.campa: Cyrus gathers the Persians and sets them a day's labor clearing a thorn-choked waste, brutal, back-breaking toil. Next day he feasts them on slaughtered flocks, with wine and every good thing, and asks which day they preferred. All choose the feast. Then, he says, choose me: obey me and you have days like this and freedom besides; refuse and you have endless labors like yesterday, under the Mede. They swear to follow. He raises the standard of revolt.
stops.quote: If you will be ruled by me, you will have these good things and ten thousand more, with no servile labor; but if you will not, you will have labors like yesterday's without number.
suggested_refs: Herodotus 1.125-126, the parable of the two days
The Persian tribes list (Herodotus 1.125): Pasargadae, Maraphii, Maspii

stops.name: The plain of Hyrba, first blood against the Medes
stops.campa: Astyages, hearing of the rising, arms the Medes and, in a madness the historians call god-sent, puts Harpagus in command of the very army meant to crush Cyrus. The hosts meet. According to the tale of the frontier, the Persians hold against the first Median assault; the war will run three years. Harpagus and a great part of the nobility, as promised, go over to Cyrus in the field. The Median host breaks apart from within.
suggested_refs: Battle of Hyrba (Ctesias / Nicolaus of Damascus tradition)
The defection of Harpagus, Herodotus 1.127

stops.name: Ecbatana taken, Astyages in chains
stops.campa: In the third year Cyrus routs the last Median levies near the field that will become Pasargadae, and takes Ecbatana itself. Astyages is led out a prisoner to the grandson he ordered killed as an infant. Cyrus does not kill him; he keeps the old king by him to the end of his days. The seven walls with their coloured battlements, the treasure of the Medes, the empire, all pass to the Persian. The vassal is now the master; Media and Persia are one crown. The Babylonian Chronicle records the day: Astyages taken, Ecbatana plundered, the spoil carried to Anshan.
stops.quote: He mustered his army and marched against Cyrus, king of Anshan... The army rebelled against Astyages and he was taken prisoner. They handed him over to Cyrus.
stops.quote_source: The Nabonidus Chronicle, ii.1-4 (fall of Astyages, 550 BC)
suggested_refs: The Nabonidus Chronicle (British Museum)
Ecbatana / Hamadan, the seven-walled Median capital

stops.name: Pasargadae founded, the city on the field of victory
stops.campa: On the high plain where he broke the Medes, Cyrus founds his city, Pasargadae, and names it for his own tribe. Here rise the great gardens, the fourfold watered paradise, the pillared palaces with their guardian figures. Here he will keep the royal fire and here he will be buried. The Persian who was a herdsman's foster-son now sits where Astyages sat, King of the Medes and the Persians, master of the Iranian plateau, and turns his eyes west and south to the older, richer kingdoms of the world.
suggested_refs: Pasargadae, the Achaemenid garden-capital (UNESCO World Heritage)
The winged genius relief at Pasargadae (Gate R)

segments.name: Croesus and the Fall of Lydia: the West

stops.name: Delphi, the oracle that ruins Croesus
stops.campa: In Sardis, Croesus of Lydia, richest of kings, who once asked Solon who was happiest of men and was told to call no man happy till he is dead, weighs war on the rising Persian. He sends gold beyond counting to Delphi and asks Apollo whether to march. The Pythia answers: if Croesus crosses the Halys he will destroy a great empire. He hears his own victory. He does not hear that the empire to fall may be his own. So the oracle, true and double-tongued, sends him east against Cyrus.
stops.quote: If Croesus should send an army against the Persians he would destroy a great empire.
stops.quote_source: The Delphic oracle to Croesus, Herodotus, Histories 1.53
suggested_refs: The Temple of Apollo at Delphi; the Pythia
Croesus's gold dedications at Delphi (Herodotus 1.50-51)

stops.name: The Halys river crossed, Pteria and the drawn battle
stops.campa: Croesus crosses the Halys, the river that was the border of Lydia and Media, and burns Pteria in Cappadocia. Cyrus marches up to meet him. They fight a whole hard day and neither breaks; night parts them undecided. Croesus, his army the smaller, judges the season too late for a second field and pulls back to Sardis to winter and gather allies, Egypt, Babylon, Sparta, for the spring. He disbands his mercenaries. He believes he has time. He does not.
suggested_refs: Kerkenes Dağ / Pteria in Cappadocia
The Halys (Kızılırmak) as the Lydo-Median boundary

stops.name: Sardis besieged, the camels against the horse
stops.campa: Cyrus does not winter. He drives straight after Croesus to the Lydian plain before Sardis, where the famed Lydian cavalry waits. On Harpagus's counsel he sets his baggage-camels in the front line: the Lydian horses, unable to bear the smell and sight of camels, wheel and bolt. The riders fight on foot and are beaten back inside the walls. The great citadel on its cliff seems impregnable; the siege closes in. Croesus, who thought himself the happiest of men, is shut in his own capital.
suggested_refs: The acropolis of Sardis on Mount Tmolus
Herodotus 1.80, the camel stratagem against Lydian cavalry

stops.name: Sardis taken: Croesus on the pyre, saved by the rain
stops.campa: On the fourteenth day a Persian scales the one unguarded cliff and the city falls. Croesus is taken and set on a great pyre with fourteen Lydian youths to burn. As the fire is lit he cries three times the name of Solon, and Cyrus asks why. Told of the Athenian's word, that no man is happy till his end, Cyrus is shaken and calls to quench the flames; but they have caught. Then Croesus prays aloud to Apollo, and out of a clear sky the god sends a black storm and a downpour that drowns the fire. Cyrus takes him down and keeps him ever after.
stops.quote: O Solon, Solon, Solon!
stops.quote_source: Croesus on the pyre, Herodotus, Histories 1.86
suggested_refs: Attic red-figure amphora by Myson, Louvre G197, Croesus on the pyre
Herodotus 1.86-87, Apollo's rain quenches the fire

stops.name: Ionia and the sea-cities subdued, Harpagus in the west
stops.campa: With Lydia fallen, the Greek cities of Ionia that would not come to terms are given to Harpagus. City by city he takes them: Phocaea, whose people rather sail away into exile than bow; Teos likewise; the rest by mound and ram. The Persians who once herded on a bare plateau now stand on the Aegean shore. Cyrus himself turns back east: the frontier of his new empire runs to the sea, and there are older thrones still to take. The map of the world is being redrawn under one crown.
suggested_refs: The flight of the Phocaeans (Herodotus 1.164-165)
Harpagus's Ionian and Carian campaign, Herodotus 1.162-176

segments.name: The Eastern Lands: the empire to the sunrise

stops.name: Return to Ecbatana, the throne of the two peoples
stops.campa: Cyrus comes back to the Median summer-capital, now his own, and orders the vast middle of his realm. He leaves Lydia in a Persian's charge, weathers a Lydian revolt and puts it down without a massacre, and forbids the burning of the sanctuaries. Ecbatana, Susa, Pasargadae: the royal roads begin to bind them. Then he sets his face to the sunrise, to the peoples the Greeks scarcely name: Parthia, Aria, Bactria, Sogdiana, the edge of the steppe.
suggested_refs: The Achaemenid royal road network
The four capitals: Pasargadae, Ecbatana, Susa, Babylon

stops.name: Hyrcania and Parthia, the first eastern peoples
stops.campa: East of the Caspian gates Cyrus passes down into Hyrcania of the wolves and Parthia of the horsemen, the near marches of the sunrise. The tradition gives these lands no siege and no slaughter: they come in under the crown as the shadow of the empire lengthens over them. He binds them as satrapies, sets Persian garrisons and Iranian governors, and does not tear down their fire-shrines. The realm now reaches from the Aegean surf to the rim of the great steppe, and no ruler in the memory of the world has held so much.
suggested_refs: Hyrcania (Gorgan plain) south-east of the Caspian
The satrapy list of the Behistun inscription of Darius

stops.name: Bactria and Sogdiana, the far satrapies bound in
stops.campa: Cyrus rides east into the great highland provinces: Parthia, Drangiana, Aria, Chorasmia, Bactria of the fine horses, Sogdiana beyond the Oxus, the Sattagydae and Gandara toward the Indus. The tradition gives no battles by name here, only the fact of it: he brings the whole Iranian east under the crown. He founds a chain of frontier posts, among them Cyropolis, the Farthest City, on the Jaxartes, to hold the line against the nomads of the outer steppe.
suggested_refs: Cyropolis (Kurushkath) on the Jaxartes / Syr Darya
Achaemenid Bactria and the satrapy list of the Behistun inscription

stops.name: Cyropolis on the Jaxartes, the Farthest City
stops.campa: On the far river the Greeks call the Jaxartes, at the very rim of the settled world, Cyrus plants the greatest of his eastern foundations and gives it his own name: Cyropolis, Kurushkath, the city of Cyrus. Beyond it lie only the horse-nomads of the open grass, the Sacae and the Massagetae, whom no plough has touched and no king has ruled. Here the empire meets the steppe. Here, one day, the steppe will meet him. He turns now to the last great throne left standing in the west: Babylon.
suggested_refs: Cyropolis, later besieged by Alexander (Arrian, Anabasis 4)
The Jaxartes (Syr Darya) as the Achaemenid northeastern limit

segments.name: The Fall of Babylon: the diverted river and the writing on the wall

stops.name: Opis on the Tigris, the Babylonian army routed
stops.campa: In the month Tashritu, Cyrus meets the army of Nabonidus at Opis on the Tigris and shatters it. The Babylonians flee; the road to the great city lies open. Nabonidus, who has spent ten years far off at the oasis of Teima worshipping the moon-god Sin while his son Belshazzar holds the capital, has neglected Marduk and the New Year rite, and the priesthood of Babylon is already half turned toward the deliverer from the east. The Chronicle marks the day of the slaughter.
stops.quote: In the month of Tashritu, when Cyrus attacked the army of Akkad at Opis on the Tigris, the inhabitants of Akkad revolted, but he massacred the people.
suggested_refs: The Battle of Opis, 539 BC
The Nabonidus Chronicle, British Museum

stops.name: Sippar surrenders, Nabonidus in flight
stops.campa: Two weeks after Opis, on the fourteenth of Tashritu, the ancient city of Sippar of the sun-god falls to Cyrus without a battle. Nabonidus, the last king of Babylon, flees the field and the city both. The whole of Akkad comes over. Only the great walls of Babylon herself still stand between Cyrus and the crown of the oldest kingdom of the earth: walls a hundred cubits high, a river running through the midst of the city, gates of bronze that the prophet in exile has already been told will be opened.
stops.quote: On the fourteenth day Sippar was captured without a battle. Nabonidus fled.
suggested_refs: Sippar (Tell Abu Habbah), city of Shamash
The Nabonidus Chronicle

stops.name: Babylon, Belshazzar's feast and the hand upon the wall
stops.campa: That night, within the doomed city, Belshazzar the prince holds a great feast for a thousand of his lords and drinks wine from the gold vessels his fathers carried off from the Temple in Jerusalem. As they praise their gods of gold and stone, fingers of a man's hand come out and write upon the plaster of the wall over against the lampstand. The king's face changes; his knees knock together. The wise men cannot read it. Daniel is brought: the writing is MENE MENE TEKEL UPHARSIN: numbered, numbered, weighed, divided. In that night the kingdom is given to the Medes and Persians.
stops.quote: MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN. This is the interpretation: God hath numbered thy kingdom, and finished it; thou art weighed in the balances, and art found wanting; thy kingdom is divided, and given to the Medes and Persians.
suggested_refs: Rembrandt, Belshazzar's Feast (National Gallery, London)
The vessels of the Jerusalem Temple, carried off by Nebuchadnezzar (Daniel 5:2-4)

stops.name: Babylon: the Euphrates diverted, the city entered in a night
stops.campa: Cyrus's men, so Herodotus tells, turn the Euphrates aside into a marsh basin upstream; the water in the channel through the city sinks to the thigh, and the Persians wade in along the dry riverbed under the walls. The gates to the river, carelessly left open in the night of the feast, betray the city. Babylon is so vast that those in the centre are dancing at the festival, taken, before the outer quarters know the enemy is within. The general Gubaru (Ugbaru) of Gutium enters with the army of Cyrus, and no battle is fought.
stops.quote: Ugbaru, governor of Gutium, and the army of Cyrus entered Babylon without a battle.
suggested_refs: Herodotus 1.191, the diversion of the Euphrates
The Ishtar Gate of Babylon (Pergamon Museum)

stops.name: Babylon: Cyrus enters in peace, the Cylinder proclaimed
stops.campa: On the third of Arahsamnu, Cyrus himself enters Babylon. Green branches are spread before him; there is no plunder, no burning. He takes the hand of Bel-Marduk in the New Year rite and is proclaimed king of the four quarters. On a clay barrel his scribes write his charter to the world: Marduk sought a righteous king and chose Cyrus of Anshan; he entered Babylon as a friend; he freed the peoples of their bondage and sent the captured gods and displaced nations home to their own places. The Jews in exile hear that their turn has come.
stops.quote: I am Cyrus, king of the world, great king, mighty king, king of Babylon, king of Sumer and Akkad, king of the four quarters... When I went as harbinger of peace into Babylon I founded my sovereign residence within the palace amid celebration and rejoicing.
suggested_refs: The Cyrus Cylinder (British Museum, ANE 90920)
The processional way and Ishtar Gate of Babylon

segments.name: The Anointed of the Lord: the captives set free

stops.name: Babylon, the gods and the peoples sent home
stops.campa: The first act of the new king is to undo the gathering of captives that the kings of Babylon had made. The statues of the gods that Nabonidus dragged into the city, from Ashur and Susa, from Akkad, Eshnunna, Zamban, Der, all the shrines across the Tigris, Cyrus sends back unharmed to their own sanctuaries, and rebuilds the ruined temples. And with the gods he sends the peoples: he gathers all the displaced nations that Babylon had uprooted and returns them, each to its own settlement. Into this great homing of captives the exiles of Judah are folded, and their turn comes with the rest.
stops.quote: I returned the images of the gods, who had resided there, to their places and I let them dwell in eternal abodes. I gathered all their inhabitants and returned to them their dwellings.
suggested_refs: The Cyrus Cylinder (British Museum), the return of gods and peoples
Livius translation of the Cyrus Cylinder

stops.name: Babylon, the edict of return proclaimed
stops.campa: In the first year of his reign over Babylon, the Lord stirs the spirit of Cyrus, and he sends a proclamation through all his kingdom, and writes it also: the God of heaven has given him all the kingdoms of the earth and charged him to build a house at Jerusalem. Let the people of that God go up; let their neighbours help them with silver and gold and beasts and freewill offerings for the house. So the word goes out that is the exact answer to seventy years of weeping by the rivers of Babylon.
stops.quote: Thus saith Cyrus king of Persia, The LORD God of heaven hath given me all the kingdoms of the earth; and he hath charged me to build him an house at Jerusalem, which is in Judah. Who is there among you of all his people? ... let him go up.
suggested_refs: Ezra 1; 2 Chronicles 36:22-23
The Cyrus Cylinder as parallel to the biblical edict

stops.name: Babylon, the vessels of the Temple restored
stops.campa: Cyrus commands the treasurer Mithredath to bring out the vessels of the house of the Lord that Nebuchadnezzar carried off from Jerusalem and set in the house of his gods: the very gold cups Belshazzar profaned at his last feast. They are counted out to Sheshbazzar, prince of Judah: chargers of gold and silver, basins, knives, bowls, five thousand four hundred vessels in all. The plunder of the fallen Temple is handed back for the Temple to come. What the moon-drunk kings of Babylon took, the anointed of the east returns.
stops.quote: Cyrus the king brought forth the vessels of the house of the LORD, which Nebuchadnezzar had brought forth out of Jerusalem, and had put them in the house of his gods.
suggested_refs: Ezra 1:7-11, the inventory of restored vessels
Sheshbazzar, prince of Judah

stops.name: Jerusalem, the foundations of the Second Temple laid
stops.campa: The exiles go up, some fifty thousand, with Zerubbabel and Jeshua the priest, on the long road from Babylon to the ruined city. In the seventh month they set the altar on its old base and offer the burnt sacrifice; in the second year they lay the Temple's foundation. The priests sound trumpets, the Levites clash cymbals and sing that the Lord is good; the young shout for joy, while the old men who saw the first house weep aloud, so that weeping and shouting cannot be told apart. Isaiah's word is fulfilled: Cyrus is the Lord's shepherd, his anointed, who says of the Temple, let it be built.
stops.quote: Thus saith the LORD to his anointed, to Cyrus, whose right hand I have holden, to subdue nations before him... even saying to Jerusalem, Thou shalt be built; and to the temple, Thy foundation shall be laid.
suggested_refs: The Second Temple (Zerubbabel's Temple), Jerusalem
Isaiah 44:28-45:13, Cyrus named a century and a half before

stops.name: Susa: the older Elamite throne, the roads made one
stops.campa: Cyrus takes into his empire the ancient Elamite seat of Susa on the lowland rivers, joining it to Anshan as of old, so that the twin heartland of Elam is whole again under one king. From Susa the royal road will one day run to Sardis. He has bound the plateau and the two great river-lands and the sea-coast into a single realm larger than any before it, and he has ruled it not by terror but, the nations say, by giving each people its own gods and its own law. He is called father.
suggested_refs: Susa, the Achaemenid winter capital
The Royal Road from Susa to Sardis (Herodotus 5.52-53)

segments.name: The Massagetae and the Last Frontier: the head in the blood

stops.name: The Araxes frontier, the marriage refused
stops.campa: Beyond the last river, on the open steppe, rule the Massagetae: horse-nomads who drink no wine, know no farming, and worship only the sun, to whom they sacrifice the swiftest of horses. Their queen is Tomyris, a widow. Cyrus, master of half the world, sends to ask her hand: meaning not the woman but the kingdom. She sees through it and refuses. So Cyrus prepares to take by the sword what he could not take by the ring, and begins to bridge the Araxes to carry his army across into her land.
stops.quote: King of the Medes, cease to press this matter... Rule your own people, and endure to see me ruling mine.
suggested_refs: The Massagetae of the Central Asian steppe
Herodotus 1.204-206, the embassy of Cyrus to Tomyris

stops.name: Across the Araxes, the banquet-trap and the capture of Spargapises
stops.campa: Tomyris offers to withdraw three days' march and let Cyrus cross to fight on her ground, or to do the same herself. On Croesus's counsel Cyrus crosses and lays a trap: he leaves his camp with a feast spread and much wine, and the weakest of his troops in it, then withdraws. A third of the Massagetae fall on the camp, kill the guards, and, knowing nothing of wine, gorge and grow drunk. The Persians return and slaughter or take them sleeping. Among the captured is Spargapises, the queen's son and the army's commander.
suggested_refs: Herodotus 1.207-211, the stratagem of the wine
The Massagetae's ignorance of wine, Herodotus 1.211

stops.name: The steppe, the death of Spargapises and the oath of Tomyris
stops.campa: Spargapises wakes from the wine to find himself a prisoner. He begs to be unbound, and the moment his hands are free he kills himself, unable to bear the shame. Tomyris, hearing that her son is dead and her army tricked with the drug the Persians call wine, sends Cyrus a herald with a terrible oath: sun-glutton, do not boast; give me back my son and go, or I swear by the Sun, lord of the Massagetae, I will give you your fill of blood.
stops.quote: Give me back my son and leave my country unharmed... If you will not, I swear by the sun, the lord of the Massagetae, that I will give you your fill of blood, insatiable as you are.
suggested_refs: Herodotus 1.211-213
The suicide of Spargapises

stops.name: The last battle: Cyrus falls, and the head in the wineskin
stops.campa: The two hosts join in the fiercest battle Herodotus knows of between barbarians. They stand and shoot until the arrows are spent, then close with spear and dagger and grapple hand to hand for a long time, neither yielding. At last the Massagetae prevail; the great part of the Persian army is destroyed, and Cyrus himself is killed, after twenty-nine years of reign. Tomyris seeks his body among the dead, fills a skin with human blood, and thrusts his severed head into it, making good her oath: glut yourself on blood, of which you could never have enough.
stops.quote: Though I live and conquer you, you have destroyed me still, for you took my son by guile; but I will make good my threat, and give you your fill of blood.
stops.quote_source: Tomyris over the head of Cyrus, Herodotus, Histories 1.214
suggested_refs: Rubens, The Head of Cyrus Brought to Queen Tomyris (Museum of Fine Arts, Boston)
Herodotus 1.214, the death of Cyrus and the vessel of blood

stops.name: Pasargadae: the tomb, and the plea to the passer-by
stops.campa: His body is brought home, the traditions say, to Pasargadae, the city he raised on the field where he first became king. There he is laid in the plain stone house on its six great steps: no vast pyramid, no boast in bronze, only a small chamber holding a golden bed and coffin and the king's ornaments, guarded by the Magi. Upon it, the Greeks record, stands the inscription that speaks to every man who will ever pass: I am Cyrus, who won the empire for the Persians; do not grudge me this little earth that covers my body. Two centuries on, Alexander stands here, reads it, and weeps.
stops.quote: O man, whoever you are and wherever you come from, for I know you will come — I am Cyrus, who won for the Persians their empire. Do not therefore begrudge me this little earth that covers my body.
